description: We are a multidisciplinary team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the Space Mission Design Game. Our goal is to create an interactive educational experience that allows users to design space missions while balancing spacecraft mass, fuel requirements, delta-v, power consumption and mission costs. We welcome passionate individuals interested in aerospace, mechanical engineering, coding, game development, UI/UX design and scientific visualization.
summary:
Mission Control is a browser based design game built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players take on the role of mission architect, allocating a limited pool of mass, power, fuel, and budget across a lunar landing, Mars rover, or satellite deployment scenario, then find out whether their design actually survives the trip.

What sets it apart is what happens next. Mid-mission, an unscripted event tests whatever margin the player kept in reserve, and every result — success or failure — gets matched to a real NASA mission that faced the same pressure. Cut your power margin too thin, and you might see echoes of a mission that hit the same problem decades earlier.

The constraints aren't invented. They're calibrated against NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool, the Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art Report, and mission data from the NSSDCA. We built this because the hardest part of engineering has never been the math — it's learning to feel a trade-off before you've made one.
details:
What it does: players pick an objective — lunar landing, Mars rover deployment, or satellite placement — then divide a fixed resource pool across mass, power, fuel, and budget using a slider interface. The game checks that allocation against the physical and financial limits a real mission would face.

How it works: partway through a run, an unscripted event — a solar flare, an underperforming launch, a late payload increase — forces a response using whatever margin the player built in. The outcome is then matched to a real NASA mission that faced the same pressure, so losing teaches something specific instead of just telling the player to try again.

Benefits: for students, it builds intuition for systems-engineering trade-offs before they ever see the formulas. For educators, it's a classroom activity that needs no lab and no aerospace background. For us, it turned a hackathon idea into something we think keeps teaching value after the event ends.

What we hope to achieve: a lightweight, approachable way to make the hardest part of mission design — trading one constraint for another under pressure — something anyone can feel, not just read about.

Tools used: the constraint logic is grounded in NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) for trajectory and fuel cost, NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art Report for mass and power ranges, and NSSDCA mission data for lunar and Mars budget figures. The demo presentation was built with help from an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), used for drafting text and generating the slide layout — the challenge selection and design decisions were our own.

Creativity: most resource trade-off tools stop at pass or fail. We wanted losing to be as informative as winning, so every outcome is tied to a real NASA mission that faced the same choice — the margin that saved it, or the shortfall that didn't.
